source.title: Neuron-Guided Interpretation of Code LLMs: Where, Why, and How?
source.authors: Zhe Yin; Xiao-Dong Gu; Bei-Jun Shen

page_placements.theme: Small selected neuron sets causally control or predict specific behaviours beyond random controls

record.tranche_reason: The paper uses identified language-specific neurons to guide fine-tuning, but does not test the claim versions about single-job neuron poles, explanation accuracy, or neuron-based attribution graphs. Its ablation experiments test language-specific function in code models, a related but different question.
record.gate_note: The paper reports language-specific neuron ablations and layer-wise probes. The ablation rows below record matched-language PLS ablations and random-ablation controls as related findings about neuron function, not tests of the listed claim versions. Table 2 also reports cross-language effects and language-agnostic neuron ablations; these are not included as rows because they do not measure any listed version. Table 1's LAPE results are a preliminary comparison, not a test of the claim versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses a gradient-based score (PLS) to find sets of programming-language-specific neurons in Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-Coder-32B. It checks them by ablation against equal-size random ablations, then uses them to guide fine-tuning. It never assigns explanations to individual neurons, measures what share have one main job, scores explanations by simulation, revisits InceptionV1, or builds attribution graphs. Its ablations show that neuron sets matter causally for a language, which is a related but different construct from per-neuron monosemanticity. The authors note neurons may be polysemous but do not measure it.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude code LLMs hold small language-specific neuron sets plus a language-agnostic set whose ablation drops pass@3 to 0%. They also find middle 'concept layers' that are semantically invariant with low syntactic decodability. Using both yields gains in fine-tuning, clone detection and summarization. They acknowledge neuron polysemy may leave interpretations incomplete.
record.recipe_differences: The paper uses a gradient-based Programming Language Specialization score and code-generation ablations, rather than auditing human-readable neuron-pole explanations. Its downstream use is neuron-guided fine-tuning.
record.method_sensitivity: Ablation effects vary by model and programming language; the paper reports especially large model-dependent differences for Python/JavaScript collateral effects.

fits_no_version.finding: Ablating small PLS-identified language-specific neuron sets (under 0.7% of neurons) sharply cuts pass@3 in the matched language. Examples: Go in Qwen2.5-Coder-32B falls 94.0%; C++ in Llama-3.1-8B falls 85.9%. Equal-size random ablations usually cut less, but not uniformly: Python random ablation in Qwen cuts 28.6%. Collateral effects on related languages are model-dependent.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Small neuron sets selected by activation×gradient attribution carry causally specific, programming-language-selective function in code LLMs.

record.problems: The authors note that individual neurons may be polysemous, leaving interpretations incomplete or imprecise; they also identify limited generalizability from two dense architectures and five programming languages. The paper notes the absence of a standard interpretability ground truth.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 has further cross-language collateral-ablation results and language-agnostic neuron-set results; omitted because they are not measures of any listed claim version. Table 1 reports preliminary LAPE ablations, also not a test of the listed versions. No listed version has a corresponding extracted result.

untested.parts: No Qwen3-32B neuron-pole audit and no one-job, two-job or unexplained shares.
Two dense models are studied, but no shares of interpretable neurons are measured. MoE and trillion-parameter scale are not tested.
No InceptionV1 or canonical polysemantic neuron is re-examined. No pose or recursive-generalization analysis.
No interpretable-share estimates and no comparison of architecture, regularization or tools.
No attribution graphs and no comparison with replacement models.
Explanations from activating examples are never checked against held-out firing.

record.verdict_notes: The record omits RQ2 (RSA and AST probes) and RQ3 (downstream task results). Neither bears on any version, so this is fine. A T4/T6 boundary case: the study does not cite or use the 'neurons are clean' essay, but it relies on neuron-level functional specificity for its fine-tuning method.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not audit Qwen3-32B neuron poles, estimate shares with one or multiple jobs, or report an unresolved share.
It studies two dense code models, but does not measure the claimed job-share estimates across models, MoE architectures, or trillion-parameter scales.
No InceptionV1 cat-and-car example, shared-pose explanation, or recursive-generalization claim is tested.
It does not estimate interpretable-neuron shares for vision models or compare architecture, regularization, and tool quality as causes of those shares.
It does not build attribution graphs or test whether neuron-based graphs explain behavior without a replacement model or reconstruction error.
It does not test neuron explanations on activating examples against held-out firing predictions.
It does not score neuron explanations by simulating activations on new text or report automated explanation-score rates.

relation.reason: Neuron sets are used as a tool; the claim about clean neuron-pole explanations is not tested.

tranche.reason: Paper uses its own gradient-based PLS score and ablations, and uses the neuron sets to guide fine-tuning. It does not audit neuron explanations.

source_check.notes: All 20 rows match Table 2 (base models, HumanEval-X pass@3). Table gives Llama Go drop -87.7%, text says 87.8%. Authors flag neuron polysemy as a limitation but do not measure it. No verdicts listed, none needed.

statements.correction: Text: language-specific neurons total under 0.7% (Llama-3.1-8B) and 0.5% (Qwen2.5-Coder-32B). Matched-language pass@3 drops: Go in Qwen -94.0%, C++ in Llama -85.9%; drops range from -18.6% (Qwen JavaScript) to -94.0%. Random ablation cut less than PLS in all 10 matched cells, though Qwen Python random still -28.6%.
